subject: Mathematics
source: Drive: Maths folder, Year 8 Maths LTP (Autumn sequence: transformations, working with numbers, percentage changes, graphs) and SOW Maths (year 8_9 scheme); aligned to the National Curriculum KS3 and Edexcel GCSE (9-1)

lessons.title: Reflections
objectives: Reflect a point or shape in a mirror line, including on a coordinate grid
Describe a reflection fully

keywords.def: a transformation that flips a shape in a mirror line
the line a shape is reflected in
the original shape and the shape after transformation
exactly the same shape and size

starter: Say Bismillah. Plot (2, 3), (-1, 4) and (-3, -2) on a grid.
What is the equation of the line through (0, 2), (1, 2) and (5, 2)?
Name the shape with 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.

teach.heading: What a reflection does
bullets: Each point is the same distance from the mirror line.
The object and image are on opposite sides.
The image is congruent to the object.
teach.note: Use a mirror or tracing paper. The line joining a point and its image is perpendicular to the mirror line. Orientation is reversed but size is unchanged.

teach.heading: Reflecting in the axes
bullets: Reflect in the y-axis: x changes sign.
teach.note: Triangle with vertices (1, 1), (1, 3), (3, 1) reflected in the y-axis gives (-1, 1), (-1, 3), (-3, 1). Ask what changes when reflecting in the x-axis (the y-coordinate).

teach.heading: Mirror lines x = a and y = b
bullets: x = 4 is a vertical line through 4.
Reflect (1, 2) in x = 4: 3 units left, so 3 units right.
teach.note: Count the distance to the line, then count the same distance on the other side. Another: reflect (4, 1) in y = 3: 2 below the line so 2 above: (4, 5).

teach.heading: The line y = x
bullets: Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates.
Draw the line first and check by eye.
teach.note: Use a diagonal line on the grid. Pupils can use tracing paper to check. The line y = x makes a 45 degree angle with the axes.

teach.heading: Describing a reflection
bullets: Say 'reflection' and give the mirror line.
Example: reflection in the line x = 2.
Give the equation, not 'the y line'.
teach.note: A full description needs the type and the equation of the mirror line. Show why saying 'reflect' alone is not enough marks in an exam.

practice: Reflect (5, -1) in the x-axis. Reflect (-4, 2) in the y-axis.
Reflect (1, 6) in the line x = 3.
Reflect (2, 7) in the line y = x.
independent: Triangle A has vertices (2, 1), (2, 4), (5, 1). Reflect it in the y-axis and write the new coordinates.
Reflect triangle A in the line y = -1 and write the new coordinates.
Reflect triangle A in the line y = x and write the new coordinates.
A shape is mapped from (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 2) to (-1, 1), (-3, 1), (-1, 2). Describe the transformation.
lessons.homework: Draw a shape of your own on a coordinate grid and reflect it in the x-axis, the y-axis and the line y = x.
lessons.send: SEND: tracing paper and mirror, pre-drawn grids. EAL: pre-teach object/image/mirror line. Stretch: reflect in lines such as y = -x.

lessons.title: Rotations
objectives: Rotate a shape about a point through a given angle and direction
Describe a rotation fully

keywords.def: a turn about a fixed point
the fixed point a shape turns about
the same direction as the hands of a clock
the opposite direction to the hands of a clock

starter: Say Bismillah. Reflect (3, -2) in the x-axis.
How many degrees in a quarter turn? In a half turn?
What is the equation of the y-axis?

teach.heading: Three things to give
teach.note: Use tracing paper: put a pencil on the centre and turn. A 180 degree turn needs no direction. Everything except the centre moves.

teach.heading: Rotating about the origin
teach.note: Also 90 degrees anticlockwise: (x, y) goes to (-y, x), so (2, 1) goes to (-1, 2). Check with tracing paper. These rules are useful but pupils should understand them, not just memorise.

teach.heading: Rotating about another point
teach.note: Work out how far the point is from the centre, rotate that vector, then add to the centre: (1 + 2, 1 - 3) = (3, -2). Check with tracing paper.

teach.heading: Describing a rotation
bullets: Example: rotation of 90 degrees clockwise about (0, 0).
Use tracing paper to find the centre.
teach.note: For an exam, all four parts earn marks. Show a pair of shapes and find the centre by trial with tracing paper: the centre is a point which stays in place.

practice: Rotate (4, 1) by 90 degrees clockwise about the origin.
Rotate (3, -2) by 180 degrees about the origin.
Rotate (2, 5) by 90 degrees anticlockwise about the origin.
independent: Triangle with vertices (1, 1), (1, 3), (3, 1). Rotate it 90 degrees clockwise about the origin and list the new vertices.
Rotate the same triangle 180 degrees about the origin.
Rotate (5, 2) by 90 degrees anticlockwise about (2, 2).
The point (2, 1) maps to (1, -2). Describe the rotation about the origin.
exit: Rotate (3, 1) by 90 degrees anticlockwise about the origin.
Rotate (-2, 4) by 180 degrees about the origin.
lessons.homework: Draw an arrow shape on a grid and rotate it by 90 and 180 degrees about a point of your choice. Write what you notice.
lessons.send: SEND: tracing paper, pre-drawn grids with centre marked. EAL: pre-teach clockwise/anticlockwise. Stretch: find the centre of rotation when given an object and its image.

lessons.title: Translations
objectives: Translate a shape using a column vector
Describe a translation fully

keywords.def: a slide of a shape without turning or flipping it
numbers written in brackets one above the other showing movement across and up
the translation that moves the image back to the object

starter: Say Bismillah. Rotate (2, 3) by 180 degrees about the origin.

teach.heading: Sliding a shape
bullets: Every point moves the same distance in the same direction.
Size, shape and direction stay the same.
teach.note: Compare with reflection and rotation, which change orientation. A translation is the only one where the shape faces the same way.

teach.heading: Column vectors
bullets: The top number: right is positive, left is negative.
The bottom number: up is positive, down is negative.
teach.note: Write the vector as a column in brackets: top number x movement, bottom number y movement. Common error: writing the numbers the wrong way round. Say 'along the corridor, then up the stairs'.

teach.heading: Translating a point
teach.note: Add the vector to the coordinates. For a shape, translate every vertex. Check that the vertices keep the same relative positions.

teach.heading: Finding the vector
teach.note: Image minus object. The inverse translation is the opposite vector: 3 right, 4 down. Pupils must write the vector as a column in the answer.

practice: Translate (3, 2) by 4 right and 5 down.
Translate the triangle (0, 0), (2, 0), (1, 3) by 3 left and 2 up.
Find the vector that maps (6, -2) to (1, 3).
independent: Translate (-2, -3) by 5 right and 4 up.
The image of a point after a translation of 2 left and 6 up is (4, -1). Find the original point.
Triangle ABC: A(1, 2), B(4, 2), C(1, 5). Translate it by 6 right and 1 down and list the new vertices.
Write the inverse of the translation 3 right and 2 down. Describe in words what happens if you apply both.
exit: Find the vector that maps (1, 1) to (4, 5).
lessons.homework: Draw a shape on a grid and translate it three times using vectors of your choice. Record each vector.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn grids, counters to move. EAL: pre-teach left/right/up/down in vector form. Stretch: combine two translations into one.

lessons.title: Describing transformations and tessellations
objectives: Describe a transformation fully
Understand and create tessellations

keywords.def: a change in the position, orientation or size of a shape
a pattern of shapes that fit together with no gaps or overlaps
angles around a point add up to 360 degrees

starter: Say Bismillah. Translate (2, 5) by 3 left and 1 down.
How many degrees do angles around a point add up to?
What is the interior angle of a square? Of an equilateral triangle?

teach.heading: Describing each transformation
bullets: Rotation: give angle, direction and centre.
teach.note: Make a summary grid. Triangle (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 2) mapped to (1, -1), (3, -1), (1, -2) is a reflection in the x-axis. Mapped to (4, 3), (6, 3), (4, 4) is a translation by 3 right and 2 up.

teach.heading: Spot the transformation
teach.note: Triangle (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 2) mapped to (-1, -1), (-3, -1), (-1, -2) is a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin. Ask pupils how they could tell.

teach.heading: Two reflections
bullets: Together this is a 180 degree rotation about the origin.
teach.note: Try with a triangle on tracing paper. This is a taste of combined transformations, a GCSE topic. Two reflections in parallel mirror lines give a translation.

teach.heading: Tessellations
bullets: Shapes tessellate if angles meet to make 360 degrees.
Squares: 4 x 90. Triangles: 6 x 60. Hexagons: 3 x 120.
Regular pentagons (108 degrees) do not tessellate.
teach.note: 360 ÷ 108 is not a whole number. Regular octagons (135 degrees) do not tessellate alone but do with squares: 135 + 135 + 90 = 360. Show examples of geometric patterns in Islamic art, which use tessellation, reflection and rotation extensively.

practice: Triangle (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 2) maps to (1, -1), (3, -1), (1, -2). Describe the transformation.
Why do equilateral triangles tessellate?
Reflect (4, 1) in the x-axis and then in the y-axis. What single transformation does this equal?
independent: Describe the transformation: (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 2) maps to (-1, 1), (-3, 1), (-1, 2).
Describe the transformation: (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 2) maps to (4, 3), (6, 3), (4, 4).
Explain with angles why regular hexagons tessellate and regular pentagons do not.
Design a tessellating pattern using one shape and a repeated transformation. Describe the transformations you used.
exit: Name the three transformations that do not change size.
Why can't regular octagons tessellate on their own?
lessons.homework: Find a tessellating pattern on a tile, wall or fabric. Draw part of it and describe the transformations in it.
lessons.send: SEND: shape tiles to physically arrange, tracing paper. EAL: pre-teach transformation names with diagrams. Stretch: investigate which regular polygons tessellate and why.

lessons.title: Powers and roots
objectives: Calculate squares, cubes and their roots
Evaluate numbers with positive integer powers

keywords.def: shows how many times a number is multiplied by itself
the number that multiplied by itself gives the original
the number that multiplied by itself three times gives the original

starter: What is 7 x 7 and what is 8 x 8?

teach.heading: Squares and cubes
teach.note: Pupils should know squares up to 15² and cubes up to 5³ and 10³. Quick quiz: ask for 13², 14², 6³. A common error is 4³ = 12.

teach.heading: Roots reverse powers
teach.note: Link to inverse operations. Ask: what is √196? (14) What is ∛125? (5) Square roots can be positive or negative, but √ means the positive root.

teach.heading: Other powers
teach.note: The index is the number of times we use the base. Note 10⁶ has six zeros. Ask pupils to calculate 2⁶ and check with a calculator.

teach.heading: Mixed calculations and negatives
bullets: Powers come before add and subtract.
teach.note: BIDMAS: indices before multiplication and addition. The bracket matters: (-3)² squares the negative, -3² means minus (3²). Check on a calculator.

teach.heading: Estimating roots
teach.note: Use known squares as markers. √90 is about 9.5 since 90 is nearly halfway between 81 and 100. A calculator gives 9.49.

practice: Work out 13², 6³ and 2⁷.
Work out √225 and ∛27.
Between which two whole numbers does √70 lie?
independent: Evaluate with a calculator: (-4)²; -4²; (-2)³; 5⁴.
Between which two whole numbers do √150, √20 and ∛100 lie?
Find a number between 2 and 100 that is both a square number and a cube number.
exit: Between which two whole numbers does √150 lie?
lessons.homework: Make a poster of squares to 15², cubes to 5³ and powers of 2 up to 2¹⁰ with one fact about each.
lessons.send: SEND: square and cube number chart. EAL: pre-teach root/power/index. Stretch: estimate roots to 1 decimal place.

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing by powers of 10
objectives: Multiply and divide integers and decimals by powers of 10
Use powers of 10 in unit conversions

keywords.def: 10, 100, 1,000 and so on; 10 multiplied by itself
a digit to the right of the decimal point
change from one unit to another

teach.heading: Digits move, zeros don't
bullets: x 10: every digit moves one place left.
÷ 10: every digit moves one place right.
The decimal point does not move; the digits do.
teach.note: Use a place value chart. Avoid the phrase 'add a zero' for decimals: 3.4 x 10 is 34, not 3.40. Show digits shifting between columns.

teach.heading: Multiplying
teach.note: 10⁴ means shift four places. Use the chart for 7.2 x 10,000 and fill with zeros. Ask pupils to predict before showing.

teach.heading: Dividing
teach.note: Dividing makes numbers smaller; shift digits right. Include zeros as placeholders. Check by multiplying back: 0.045 x 1,000 = 45.

teach.heading: Two steps
teach.note: 3.5 x 10 ÷ 100 is a net shift of one place right. Use this for unit conversions: 4.2 km = 4,200 m (x 1,000) and 6,500 ml = 6.5 litres (÷ 1,000).

practice: Work out 6.7 x 10 and 0.082 x 100.
Work out 450 ÷ 1,000 and 3.14 x 10³.
Convert 4.2 km to metres and 6,500 ml to litres.
independent: A packet of dates weighs 0.35 kg. Find the mass of 1,000 packets in kg and in grams.
Mohammed says 4.7 x 10 = 4.70. Explain his mistake.
lessons.homework: Convert five measurements in your home (such as a 1.5 litre bottle, a 2 m door) into smaller units using powers of 10.
lessons.send: SEND: place value chart with movable digit cards. EAL: pre-teach shift/decimal point. Stretch: multiply by 10⁻² and explain.

lessons.title: Rounding to decimal places
objectives: Round numbers to a given number of decimal places
Round large numbers to the nearest power of 10

keywords.def: the position of a digit after the decimal point
replace a number by a nearby, simpler number
a value that is close but not exact

starter: Say Bismillah. Round 4,567 to the nearest 10 and 100.
Which digit is in the second decimal place of 3.472?

teach.heading: Counting decimal places
bullets: In 7.846 the 8 is the first decimal place.
The 4 is the second, and the 6 is the third.
Rounding to 2 d.p. keeps two digits after the point.
teach.note: Draw a place value chart for the decimal part. Ask: what is the value of the 4? (4 hundredths)

teach.heading: The rounding rule
bullets: Look at the next digit after the one you keep.
5 or more: round up. 4 or less: leave.
teach.note: For 1 d.p.: look at the 4, round down. For 2 d.p.: look at the 6, round up the 4 to 5. Make sure pupils do not round the already-rounded number again.

teach.heading: Tricky cases
teach.note: Carrying: 3.996 rounds up, 9 + 1 carries through. Zeros at the end of a decimal show the accuracy, so write 4.00 not 4. For 0.0749, the digit after the second d.p. is 4, so stay at 0.07.

teach.heading: Large numbers
teach.note: Same rule as in primary. Check each by looking at the digit to the right. Discuss the value of a sensible rounding in context: attendance at a match, populations.

practice: Round 5.678 to 1 d.p. and to 2 d.p.
Round 0.0451 to 2 d.p.
Round 3,847,290 to the nearest 10,000.
independent: Round 12.3456 to 1, 2 and 3 d.p.
Round to the nearest 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000: 3,847,290.
A calculator shows 17.6666666. Write it to 1, 2 and 3 d.p. and say which is most accurate.
lessons.homework: Divide 100 by 7, 8, 9 and 11 on a calculator and round each answer to 2 d.p.
lessons.send: SEND: decimal place value chart, highlight the deciding digit. EAL: pre-teach decimal place. Stretch: explain why 0.995 to 2 d.p. is 1.00.

lessons.title: Rounding to significant figures
objectives: Round numbers to a given number of significant figures
Use 1 significant figure to estimate calculations

keywords.def: a digit that tells us the size of a number, starting from the first non-zero digit
an approximate answer found by rounding
a zero used to keep other digits in the right place

teach.heading: What is a significant figure?
bullets: Start counting at the first non-zero digit.
teach.note: Leading zeros are not significant; zeros between non-zero digits are (3,046 has 4 s.f.). Contrast with decimal places, which count from the decimal point.

teach.heading: Rounding to s.f.
bullets: Fill with zeros to keep place value.
teach.note: Find the last digit to keep, look at the next, round. Use zeros as place holders for whole numbers; 45,872 is not 46. For 0.004738, the 2nd s.f. is 7, the next digit is 3, so stay at 0.0047.

teach.heading: Careful cases
teach.note: For 2.0976 to 3 s.f., the zero is the 2nd s.f. so write 2.10 (showing the accuracy). For 9.96 to 2 s.f. we get 10, which also has 2 s.f. Spend time on these as they are where marks are lost.

teach.heading: Estimating with 1 s.f.
bullets: The estimate shows the answer is sensible.
teach.note: Round each number to 1 s.f. then calculate. Make clear this is an estimate. Check: 4.87 x 21.3 = 97.4 + 6.331 = 103.731.

practice: Round 6,849 to 1 s.f.
Round 0.07382 to 2 s.f.
Estimate 3.92 x 48.7 using 1 s.f.
independent: Round 150,400 to 3 s.f. and 12.57 to 3 s.f.
Explain the difference between 2 decimal places and 2 significant figures for 0.04567.
lessons.homework: Choose five numbers from a newspaper or website. Round each to 1, 2 and 3 s.f.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight the first non-zero digit with a coloured pen. EAL: pre-teach significant. Stretch: bounds of rounded numbers.

lessons.title: Large numbers in standard form
objectives: Write large numbers in standard form and convert back
Order and multiply simple numbers in standard form

keywords.def: a number written as A x 10ⁿ with A between 1 and 10
10 multiplied by itself n times
another name for standard form

teach.heading: Why standard form?
teach.note: Scientists use standard form for distances and sizes. The speed of light is about 3 x 10⁸ metres per second.

teach.heading: The rules
teach.note: A must have exactly one non-zero digit before the decimal point. Correct 45 x 10³ to 4.5 x 10⁴. Ask pupils why 0.5 x 10⁵ is also not standard form.

teach.heading: Ordinary to standard form
teach.note: Count how many places the decimal point moves to get A between 1 and 10: that count is n. For 45,000 the point moves 4 places. Check by multiplying back.

teach.heading: Standard form to ordinary
teach.note: Move the point n places right and use zeros to fill. Also ordering: 4.1 x 10⁴ < 2.9 x 10⁵ < 3.2 x 10⁵; compare the powers first, then the A values.

teach.heading: Multiplying
teach.note: Extension: (4 x 10⁵) x (5 x 10³) = 20 x 10⁸ = 2 x 10⁹, which needs rewriting. Optional: small numbers use negative powers, 0.00045 = 4.5 x 10⁻⁴.

practice: Write 83,000 in standard form.
Write 5.2 x 10⁵ as an ordinary number.
Which is bigger: 6.1 x 10⁴ or 9.8 x 10³?
independent: Write as ordinary numbers: 2.7 x 10⁴; 6.05 x 10³; 1.2 x 10⁷.
Order smallest first: 3.2 x 10⁵; 4.1 x 10⁴; 2.9 x 10⁵.
Calculate (3 x 10³) x (2 x 10⁴) and give the answer in standard form.
exit: Write 7.2 x 10³ as an ordinary number.
lessons.homework: Find five large measurements (distances, populations) and write them in standard form.
lessons.send: SEND: place value chart showing the decimal point moving. EAL: pre-teach standard form vocabulary. Stretch: very small numbers with negative powers.

lessons.title: Percentages of amounts and simple increase and decrease
objectives: Find a percentage of an amount without a calculator
Increase and decrease an amount by a percentage

keywords.def: a fraction out of 100
make bigger by an amount
make smaller by an amount

teach.heading: Increase by a percentage
teach.note: Two steps: find the change, then add. Link to context: a price rise or a pay rise.

teach.heading: Decrease by a percentage
teach.note: Find 10% (8.5), multiply by 4 (34), subtract. Sale prices. Common mistake: giving the 34 as the answer rather than the new price.

teach.heading: A percentage in daily life: zakat
teach.note: This is a maths example only; for rulings on zakat (nisab, conditions) pupils should ask a qualified scholar. Another way: 2.5% = 1/40, and 6,000 ÷ 40 = 150.

practice: Find 12% of £350.
Increase £150 by 8%.
Decrease 64 kg by 25%.
independent: Increase £420 by 15%. Decrease £2,500 by 4%.
A £48 jacket has 30% off in a sale. What is the sale price?
A salary of £1,800 rises by 5%. What is the new salary?
lessons.homework: Find three sale prices or interest rates in a shop or bank website and calculate the new price or interest for each.
lessons.send: SEND: percentage bar models, 10% grids. EAL: pre-teach increase/decrease/off. Stretch: percentages with decimals such as 7.5% of £64.

lessons.title: Using a multiplier
objectives: Find the multiplier for a percentage increase or decrease
Use a multiplier to calculate the new amount in one step

keywords.def: the number you multiply by to apply a percentage change
the amount of increase as a percentage of the original
the value before the change

teach.heading: 100% plus the increase
teach.note: Show that 112% of the original is the new amount. The multiplier does both steps (find the change and add) in one.

teach.heading: 100% minus the decrease
teach.note: More: +30% gives 1.3, +7.5% gives 1.075, -35% gives 0.65, -2% gives 0.98. Common error: using 0.15 as the multiplier for a 15% decrease.

teach.heading: Using the multiplier
teach.note: Compare with the two-step method to check. The multiplier is efficient with a calculator and is needed for repeated change.

teach.heading: Repeated change
bullets: A car worth £8,000 loses 10% each year.
teach.note: Stretch content. It is not the same as losing 20%, which would give £6,400. Use 0.9 squared = 0.81.

practice: Write the multiplier for: +5%; -20%; +45%; -2%.
Increase £360 by 15% using a multiplier.
Decrease £90 by 35% using a multiplier.
independent: Use multipliers: 64 increased by 25%; 350 decreased by 10%; £1,200 increased by 3.5%.
A £60 bike is reduced by 18% in the sale. What is the sale price?
A population of 20,000 grows by 4% each year. Find the population after 2 years.
Explain why a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease does not return to the original amount.
exit: What is the multiplier for a 7% increase?
lessons.homework: Write multipliers for six percentage changes of your choice, then apply each to £500.
lessons.send: SEND: multiplier table linking percent, decimal and multiplier. EAL: pre-teach multiplier. Stretch: repeated percentage change with powers.

lessons.title: Calculating a percentage change
objectives: Express a change as a percentage of the original
Calculate percentage profit and loss

keywords.def: the change as a percentage of the original value
money made when selling for more than the cost
money lost when selling for less than the cost

starter: Say Bismillah. Write 30/120 as a percentage.
Write 9/45 as a fraction in its simplest form.

teach.heading: The formula
bullets: Always divide by the original value.
teach.note: Emphasise the original (starting) value. Pupils often divide by the new value. Change = new - original.

teach.heading: Increase example
teach.note: Also 40 to 50 is an increase of 10, and 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25, so 25% increase.

teach.heading: Decrease example
teach.note: Note that 80 to 60 is a 25% decrease, but 60 to 80 is a 33.3% increase: the original differs. Ask why.

teach.heading: Profit and loss
bullets: Profit percentage is on the cost price.
teach.note: Loss example: bought for £40, sold for £34; loss £6, 6 ÷ 40 = 15% loss. Link to fair trade (honest dealing in business is encouraged in Islam) only as a context, without quotations.

practice: A price rises from 50 to 65. Find the percentage increase.
A price falls from 200 to 170. Find the percentage decrease.
A trader buys for £60 and sells for £75. Find the percentage profit.
independent: Find the percentage change: 60 to 75; 250 to 200; £12 to £15.60; 1,500 to 1,320.
A population grows from 20,000 to 23,000. Find the percentage increase.
A shirt bought for £40 is sold for £34. Find the percentage loss.
Explain why a fall from 80 to 60 and a rise from 60 to 80 are different percentages.
exit: Find the percentage change from 20 to 27.
Find the percentage change from 90 to 72.
lessons.homework: Find the price of an item now and a year ago (ask family, or from a website) and calculate the percentage change.
lessons.send: SEND: formula prompt card, worked example frame. EAL: pre-teach change/original/profit/loss. Stretch: compare two percentage changes.

lessons.title: Reverse percentages
objectives: Find the original amount before a percentage change
Recognise when to divide by the multiplier

keywords.def: finding the original value from the value after a percentage change
the operation that undoes another
the starting amount before the change

starter: Say Bismillah. What is the multiplier for a 20% increase?
What is the multiplier for a 15% decrease?

teach.heading: Going backwards
bullets: After a 20% increase the price is £90.
teach.note: Take 20% off 90 to get 72 is the classic error. Because 20% of the new price is not the same as 20% of the original.

teach.heading: Divide by the multiplier
teach.note: Use the inverse operation. Also show the bar model: 120% is 90, so 10% is 7.50 and 100% is 75.

teach.heading: A sale price
teach.note: Check: 80 x 0.85 = 68. A 15% reduction on £80 is £12, giving £68.

teach.heading: Choosing the correct approach
bullets: Original given: multiply by the multiplier.
New value given: divide by the multiplier.
teach.note: Ask pupils to say which situation they are in before calculating. Practice with a mixed set where both types are present.

practice: After a 10% increase a price is £66. Find the original.
After a 25% decrease a price is £45. Find the original.
After a 5% rise a salary is £420 per week. What was it before?
independent: Find the original: £35 after 30% off; £112 after a 12% increase; £192 after a 4% decrease.
A price including 20% VAT is £144. What is the price before VAT?
A town's population grew by 6% to 31,800. What was it before?
Mina says '20% off £90 gives £72, so £90 after a 20% rise was £72.' Explain her mistake.
exit: After an 18% increase a price is £59. Find the original.
After 20% off a coat costs £48. Find the original price.
lessons.homework: Find three sale items. For each, make up the original price and sale percentage, and work backwards from the sale price to check.
lessons.send: SEND: bar model templates, multiplier cards. EAL: pre-teach original/inverse. Stretch: reverse percentages after two successive changes.

lessons.title: Graphs from linear equations
objectives: Complete a table of values for a linear equation
Plot and draw straight-line graphs

keywords.def: an equation whose graph is a straight line
a table of x values and their matching y values
a pair of numbers (x, y) that give a position

teach.heading: Table of values
bullets: Put each x value into the equation to get y.
teach.note: Full table: x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y = -3, -1, 1, 3, 5, 7. Each x increases by 1 and y increases by 2: this pattern shows a straight line.

teach.heading: Plot and join
bullets: Extend the line past the points.
teach.note: Choose a scale to fit the range. Label the line with its equation. If one point is off the line, check the calculation.

teach.heading: Another example
teach.note: This line goes down as x increases. Compare with y = 2x + 1. Link this to the gradient next lesson.

teach.heading: Special lines
bullets: y = x passes through the origin.
teach.note: x = a: every point has x-coordinate a. Pupils often mix up x = 4 and y = 4. Check by naming points on each.

teach.heading: Does a point lie on the line?
teach.note: Substitute the x value and compare with the y value. This is a quick exam skill.

practice: Complete a table for y = x + 3 for x from -2 to 2.
Complete a table for y = 4x - 1 for x from 0 to 3.
independent: Draw the graph of y = 2x - 3 for x from -1 to 3.
Draw the graph of y = 5 - 2x for x from 0 to 3.
Which of (2, 4), (0, 2), (-1, -5) lie on the line y = 3x - 2?
Draw the lines x = 3 and y = -1 on the same axes and state where they cross.
exit: Find y when x = 3 in y = x + 4.
lessons.homework: Draw the graphs of y = x + 2, y = x - 3 and y = 2x on the same axes and describe what is similar and different.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn axes, partially filled tables. EAL: pre-teach table of values/substitute. Stretch: find where two lines cross.

lessons.title: Gradient of a straight line
objectives: Calculate the gradient of a straight line from two points
Interpret positive, negative and zero gradients

keywords.def: a measure of how steep a line is; change in y divided by change in x
lines that never meet and have the same gradient
the vertical change and the horizontal change between two points

starter: Complete the table for y = 2x + 1 when x = 0, 1, 2.

teach.heading: How steep?
bullets: Rise = vertical change. Run = horizontal change.
teach.note: Draw a right-angled triangle under a line. Link to ramps and roofs. Always move left to right.

teach.heading: From two points
teach.note: Use the same order for both coordinates. A gradient of 3 means for every 1 across the line goes 3 up.

teach.heading: Negative gradients
teach.note: Going left to right, the line falls. A horizontal line has gradient 0; a vertical line has no gradient (undefined).

teach.heading: Parallel lines and equations
teach.note: Link to the tables last lesson: y = 2x + 1 rose by 2 each time x rose by 1; the gradient is 2. This leads to y = mx + c.

practice: Find the gradient between (0, 1) and (3, 10).
Find the gradient between (1, 8) and (4, 2).
Find the gradient between (2, 3) and (6, 5).
independent: Find the gradient: (0, 0) and (4, 12); (1, 7) and (3, 1); (-2, 1) and (2, 5).
State the gradient of each: y = 7x + 1; y = x - 9; y = 4 - 3x.
A line passes through (0, 2) and has gradient 3. Find two more points on it.
Are the lines through (0, 1) and (2, 5), and through (1, 0) and (4, 6), parallel?
lessons.homework: Draw three lines with gradients 1, 2 and -1. Choose two points on each and check the gradient by calculation.
lessons.send: SEND: gradient triangles on printed graphs. EAL: pre-teach steep/rise/run. Stretch: gradient as rate of change in context.

lessons.title: The equation y = mx + c
objectives: Identify the gradient and y-intercept from y = mx + c
Find the equation of a straight line from a graph or conditions

keywords.def: the point where a line crosses the y-axis
the equation of a straight line with gradient m and y-intercept c
change the form of an equation without changing its meaning

starter: Say Bismillah. Find the gradient between (0, 3) and (2, 9).

teach.heading: m and c
bullets: m is the gradient. c is the y-intercept.
teach.note: The line crosses the y-axis at (0, c) since x = 0 gives y = c. Draw y = 3x - 2 and check the gradient and intercept.

teach.heading: From a gradient and intercept
teach.note: Substitute into y = mx + c. Pupils often swap m and c. Say: 'm is the multiplier of x'.

teach.heading: From a graph
teach.note: Read c from where the line meets the y-axis, find m by drawing a triangle. Check with the second point: 3 x 2 + 1 = 7.

teach.heading: Rearranging and parallel lines
teach.note: Divide every term by 2 when rearranging. Last example: 5 = 2 x 1 + c gives c = 3. This is the stretch step.

practice: State the gradient and y-intercept of y = 2x + 5, y = x - 4 and y = 7 - 3x.
Write the equation of the line with gradient 4 and y-intercept -1.
Find the equation of the line through (0, 3) with gradient 2.
independent: Find the equation of the line through (0, -3) and (2, 1).
Rearrange 2y = 8x + 6 into the form y = mx + c.
Write the equation of a line parallel to y = 5x - 1 through (0, 6).
Is (3, 10) on y = 3x + 1? Find the equation of a line through (1, 5) with gradient 2.
exit: State the gradient and y-intercept of y = 6x - 7.
Write the equation of the line with gradient 2 through (0, 3).
lessons.homework: Write the equations of four lines with different gradients and intercepts, draw them and check the gradient and intercept of each.
lessons.send: SEND: m and c colour-coded equation cards, pre-drawn graphs. EAL: pre-teach intercept/gradient. Stretch: find the equation of a line through any two points.
